name: Bordeaux
lede: Bordeaux is the deep, slightly bluish red of the red wines of Bordeaux, a port that was also a hub of the blue-dye trade.

sections.title: A wine's color
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines *Bordeaux* as a bluish red, the color of Bordeaux wines, and lists a separate industrial *Bordeaux red* made from beta-naphthol [1]. It defines *claret* as a reddish violet that has the same hue as Bordeaux wine, and says the word comes from the Latin for clear [1]. *Burgundy*, the red of the other great French wine region, is a reddish purple that Paterson calls less blue than Bordeaux [1]. St Clair sees it differently: Bordeaux is a deep cherry and burgundy a deep purple-brown [2]. Books disagree, then, on which of the two wine reds leans further toward purple, and the safe reading is that the two are close neighbors [1][2].

The swatch here, #75343D, is a dark red in the ISCC-NBS system [3]. Ridgway's 1912 color atlas has a Bordeaux on plate XII, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates the name to about 1850 [3]. The nearest of our core colors is [[burgundy]] [3]. ISCC-NBS block 16, which this color falls in, gathers a dozen more wine names, among them Claret Wine, Old Wine, Ruby Wine, Spanish Wine, Wine Lees and Vin Rosé, whose first recorded use Maerz and Paul put at 1895 [3]. Close relatives with their own pages include [[claret]], [[maroon]], [[oxblood]] and [[merlot]] [3].

sections.title: The port of the blue trade
sections.body:
Bordeaux is also a place where blue was bought and sold, and the history is worth knowing, because the city's name sits oddly on a red. Woad grown around Toulouse in the Languedoc was shipped by barge down the Garonne to Bordeaux, which profited greatly from exporting it to Flanders, Italy, Spain and Britain [4]. Balfour-Paul gives an annual figure of 200,000 bales of woad, with madder dye, alum and wine traveling alongside it [4]. Italian merchants centered on Venice dominated the sea trade in woad, and the main route ran from Venice through Genoa, Narbonne and Bordeaux to Britain and the Low Countries [4].

When West Indian indigo arrived, the port turned to the new dye [5]. From the mid-1680s it was the most interesting commodity landing at Bordeaux and Marseilles [5]. By the 1780s the French colony of Saint-Domingue had no fewer than 3,150 indigo plantations, and indigo was a key cargo at Bordeaux, destined for French textile mills and for re-export [5]. Pastoureau adds that New World indigo was cheaper than European woad, even after the Atlantic crossing, because its production relied more and more on slavery [6]. French law finally approved indigo throughout the kingdom in 1737, which enriched Nantes, Bordeaux and Marseilles and ruined Toulouse, the woad capital [6]. The wealth also helped make blue the common color of eighteenth-century dress, as dyers learned to make lighter and more luminous blues [7]. Paterson lists a *Bordeaux blue* too, a shade of blue with no further description [1].

sections.title: Bordeaux in the dye vat and the pigment tube
sections.body:
In modern dyes and pigments *bordeaux* became a standard description for the darkest, bluest reds. The Pigment Compendium says the beta-naphthol azo pigments run from yellowish and medium reds to bordeaux, carmine, brown and violet, citing Herbst and Hunger [8]. The benzimidazolone azo pigments reach maroon, bordeaux and brown [8]. Perylene vat pigments range from red and scarlet through vermilion to bordeaux; the first were discovered by Kardos in 1912 and 1913 and by Friedlander in 1919, but they were not generally used until after 1950 [9]. Perinone pigments, discovered in 1924 by Eckert and Greune at Hoechst, were recognized as pigments only in 1950 and give orange to bordeaux shades [9].

A dye gave a name to one artist's pigment as well. A supplier's Mars violet, an iron-oxide earth, was brightened with an organic violet dye called Helio Bordeaux, which the Colour Index lists as Pigment Red 54, according to an analysis by Helwig in 1998 [10]. The Compendium notes the practice because it means such a paint is not a pure earth [10].

sections.title: The duchy's court
sections.body: The other great wine red takes its name from a duchy whose court was known for black. Philip the Good, who ruled the duchy until 1467, made black the fashion of the age at his court [11]. Chroniclers said he wore it in mourning for his father, killed in 1419, though Pastoureau treats that as only part of the story [11]. The style spread to Spain and across Europe and lasted until the middle of the seventeenth century [11]. Where to look: hold a glass of red wine up to a window, or look at dark red velvet in daylight, and watch for the bluish cast that Paterson's definition points to [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, 114 contain this color as at least five per cent of the canvas, within a ΔE of 6 [12]. Those are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is as photographed and not a pigment test [12]. The largest covers are a ragamala page of about 1750 at 59 per cent, Poussin's [[painting:commons-Q27974876|Descent from the Cross]] of about 1630 at 57 per cent, and a portrait of an official of about 1600 at 52 per cent [12]. The earliest is Lippo Memmi's *Madonna and Child with Donor* of about 1325, where it just reaches 5 per cent [12].

The color clusters in the late 1400s [12]. In the 1400s, 14 of 945 paintings hold it, about three times the average rate, and in the 1500s, 21 of 2,231 [12]. The peak decade is the 1470s, with 6 of 156 paintings, eight times the rate [12]. Our data cannot say whether the reason is dye, glaze or the way red lakes have aged, and it would be a mistake to guess [12]. By country, Italy supplies 23 of the hits, and India 8 of 721 paintings [12]. Among movements, 3 of 96 Kalighat paintings and 3 of 168 Mughal paintings hold it, about 6.5 and 3.7 times the average [12].

When it appears it is a shadow or middle tone: 47 per cent of its pixels are in the shadow band, 50 per cent in the middle and only 3 per cent in the highlights [12]. In Google Books the word *bordeaux* peaks around 1908, but the word is mostly the city and the wine, so the curve is not a history of the color [13].

questions.q: Why did Bordeaux profit from the woad and indigo trades?
choices: It was the port where the dyes were shipped out and landed
It was where woad was grown
Its wine was used to ferment the dye
questions.answer: It was the port where the dyes were shipped out and landed

questions.q: True or false: books agree exactly on how Bordeaux and burgundy differ.

openers: Bordeaux shipped woad and then indigo: the city of red wine was a port of blue.
